items.body: (Photo credit: Allen Cohen) Reaching Marlboro requires a gradual surrender of scale. Roads narrow, familiar coordinates loosen, and the forest exerts its own editorial influence, stripping away whatever feels extraneous until distance becomes a form of concentration. On September 20, 2026, that concentration gathered inside Ragle Hall at the Serkin Center, where the Marlboro Music Artist Residency Program presented The World of György Kurtág, an arresting sequence of works composed or arranged for soprano and double bass. Beyond the hall stood the wooded seclusion of southern Vermont; within it, soprano Lucy Fitz Gibbon and bassist William Langlie Miletich moved between Sprechstimme, art song, extended technique, and charged silence. Seclusion mattered because Kurtág’s music alters the proportions of attention. The claim embedded in the program’s title was stranger than its apparent simplicity suggested. The phrase “world of” ordinarily announces breadth, an oeuvre surveyed from above. Kurtág offers no such cartographic comfort. His world emerges through radical compression, forming under pressure between a sound and its possible disappearance. A few pitches can contain the moral weight of a dramatic scene. A pause can bend duration until time folds inward, secreting another time inside itself. His miniatures remain small only to the clock. To enter them is to accept unfamiliar laws under which fragments carry the mass of vanished wholes and inhalation behaves as active matter. The surrounding forest supplied an uncannily precise grammar for this experience. Every trunk concealed years in concentric script; every root continued a sentence underground. Kurtág’s art operates within a related economy of the imperceptible. A phrase ends, yet its pressure travels elsewhere. Music becomes the audible extremity of processes occurring beneath language. The sequence approached that hidden economy gently through Lembit Beecher’s With Grandchildren, drawn from his 2014 cycle Looking at Spring: Meditations on Aging. The larger work grew from interviews librettist Liza Balkan conducted with senior citizens in Toronto and central Vermont, making its appearance in Marlboro feel almost homeward. Their voices had passed into text and music before returning to the region transformed, bearing traces of their speakers without claiming to preserve them intact. Harmonics in the bass courted a rocking motion whose comfort never became secure, while Fitz Gibbon searched amid the delicate failures of memory. The soul became an unfinished sentence poised beneath scissors, family albums reduced to particles of touch and chronology. Bone creaked as marrow acquired a secret literacy, becoming a divining instrument for the inaccessible past. Beecher respected recollection as an unstable act in which forgetting shapes experience as decisively as retention. Miletich’s pale overtones gave the bass an elderly nervous system of its own. The final word escaped capture, suspending language where recognition touches disappearance. John Cage’s The Wonderful Widow of Eighteen Springs opened another passage into that borderland. Composed in 1942, its text comes from a nocturnal passage concerning Isobel in Finnegans Wake, a book of sleeping consciousness and linguistic mutation. Cage answered that abundance with severe economy. The voice circles within three pitches, while the original accompaniment is played on a closed piano tapped by the player. In Marlboro, those impulses migrated to the double bass, where Miletich turned his instrument of choice into a hollow nocturnal chamber. What had once been struck wood surrounding dormant strings now came from an assemblage held against the player’s body, each impact becoming a coded knock from somewhere inside itself. Fitz Gibbon sustained Cage’s narrow compass with remarkable intensity. Repetition wandered in place, circling a road inferred from every failed attempt to leave it. James Joyce’s words acquired the phosphorescence of objects glimpsed among trees. Isobel became a consciousness translated into the landscape, as identity passed into leaf matter and the boundary between a sleeping mind and the forest dreaming it lost authority. Amy Beth Kirsten’s yes I said yes I will Yes followed as a second excavation of Joyce, drawing on Molly Bloom’s concluding monologue in Ulysses. Written in 2012 for soprano and contrabass, with the bassist also vocalizing, it entered an illuminating dialogue with Cage. Both composers extract a concentrated vocal world from Joyce’s literary machinery. Whereas Cage cools language toward incantation, Kirsten restores its heat while fracturing the body that generates it. Isobel’s suspension yields to Molly’s consciousness in bed, where memory moves through eros and resistance before reaching the irrevocable “Yes.” Fitz Gibbon and Miletich rendered that sensuality as a condition divided against itself. Pizzicato entered beside Miletich’s droning hum, while glissandi bent the music from stable coordinates. Fitz Gibbon inhabited desire while observing its mechanisms from afar, consciousness hovering above its own flesh. The deeply inflected conclusion unfolded as slow-motion blues, each pitch bearing the drag of pleasure becoming memory before experience could have its say. These works prepared the ear for Kurtág’s Einige Sätze aus den Sudelbüchern Georg Christoph Lichtenbergs, Op. 37a, begun in 1996 and expanded for soprano and double bass in 1999. The cycle arose from his encounter with the private notebooks of Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, the 18th-century physicist whose intellect moved between experiment and satire. Never intended for publication, these “waste books” gathered observations whose brevity sharpened their reach. Lichtenberg’s scrutiny ranges across provincialism and religion, colonialism and literary history. Each joke becomes a trapdoor opening onto centuries of vanity. Kurtág began setting the aphorisms while ill, initially for solo soprano. Singer Maria Husmann encouraged the addition of double bass after experimenting with improvised accompaniment, a genesis audible in the finished cycle. Voice and instrument discover one another without settling into fixed roles. The bass accompanies before interrupting, then places a dark question mark beneath Lichtenberg’s wit. Fitz Gibbon and Miletich inhabited these relations with theatrical aptitude. The opening “Die Kartoffeln” (“The Potatoes”) was oddly beautiful in its evocation of slumbering tubers and their potential afterlife. “Kirchtürme” (“Church Spires”) rose through lovely pizzicato, its aspiration destabilized by the plucking that produced it. “Koan” became a fervent prayer edging toward cognitive seizure. Kurtág exposed the nervous system inside each of these, revealing the involuntary twitch beneath polished intelligence. That method reached sardonic clarity in “…und eine neue Welt…” (“…and a New World…”), where Fitz Gibbon sang through her teeth: “The American who discovered Columbus made a nasty discovery.” The reversal compresses colonial history into a grammatical ambush, exposing discovery as a story power tells about intrusion. Here, as elsewhere in the cycle, language appeared to turn against the assumptions concealed within its own syntax. Beecher’s stop-motion films, still a work in progress and therefore accompanying only selected aphorisms, extended this instability into a visual register. His reappearance as animator also gave the program a satisfying circular architecture. Having entered through his own music in With Grandchildren, he returned within Kurtág’s, translating acts of listening into movement and matter. Objects advanced through minute discontinuities, their apparent motion created by absences between frames. The art form therefore proved uncannily suited to Kurtág, whose music repeatedly asks the listener to construct continuity across charged gaps. Both forms make disappearance part of their syntax. The most persuasive union of image and sound came in “Ein Liebhaber der klassischen Philologie” (“A Classical Philology Aficionado”), concerning a man so enamored of Homer that he reads the German angenommen as “Agamemnon.” Books towered behind drifting clouds while statues looked on as thought acquiring mineral flesh. Beecher let the visual analog unfold slowly, giving the words time to expose the strange pathology hidden inside cultivated learning. Erudition became a benign haunting, a possession so complete that antiquity rewrote the present from within. The sequence clarified what the animations contributed to the cycle as a whole: they gave Kurtág’s microscopic dramas another surface upon which to misremember and mutate. The closing “Ein merkwürdiger Gedanke” (“A Strange Thought”) brought Kurtág’s humor to its darkest edge. Miletich and Fitz Gibbon allowed laughter to reveal its ancient kinship with fear. By then, one work had entered another through hidden roots. Cage’s knocks survived inside Kirsten’s tapping, while Beecher’s elderly voices continued inside Lichtenberg’s posthumous sentences. And through it all, Joyce’s sleeping forest returned in the Vermont woods surrounding the hall. The program cohered through subterranean recurrence, with each composition sending material below the surface for another to absorb. Marlboro’s seclusion ultimately changed the concert. Isolation became an acoustic form of relation, concentrating distant minds into one chamber. Beneath our feet, roots continued their exchanges without witnesses, each message altered by the body carrying it. The afternoon suggested that memory follows the same obscure traffic. We imagine ourselves as its custodians, although the reverse may lie closer to the truth. Memory could be the larger organism, ancient and unfinished, using each of us as a temporary organ through which to migrate. For one hour in Ragle Hall, voices became gills in that organism. The post The Forest Beneath Language: Entering the World of György Kurtág in Marlboro appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Some promotion arrives generously late, but with this debut album by the Australian solo project Empty Vessel, I felt it was more than necessary to give it some attention anyway. Tom Wojcicki is an artist unknown to most, who released the album “Ruin Value” in the spring of 2025, an opus consisting of eight tracks. What I hear here defies all imagination: an absolute masterpiece in which the artist blends Industrial, Cinematic, and Ritual elements in a remarkably refined manner. He creates a tormented atmosphere of overwhelming sounds, with percussion effects that reverberate like drones. That overwhelming quality, in particular, is almost indescribable. Rarely have I encountered an artist capable of creating sounds as intense, present, and tormented as those of Empty Vessel. The tracks can be repetitive at times, but because of their sheer intensity, you are truly blown away. Before you know it, you are trapped in a sonic web of terrifying and illusory images. The album is a succession of insane tracks, meaning that you discover one highlight after another. If you are a fan of the genres mentioned above and are not yet familiar with Empty Vessel, I would simply recommend buying this album without listening to it beforehand. An absolute masterpiece, and it will not be easy to follow this up with an equally powerful successor. (Rating:9). Listen to “Scattered Pieces Of Her”: Scattered Pieces Of Her by Empty Vessel About Empty Vessel Empty Vessel is the solo industrial and power electronics project of Australian artist Tom Wojcicki. “Ruin Value” was released on 14 April 2025 through the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen as a hand-numbered CD limited to 200 copies with a 4-page booklet, plus a digital edition, under catalog number DP179CD. The album runs eight tracks, opening with “Scattered Pieces Of Her” and closing with “Zero Fetish”. Empty Vessel has also recorded under the names Droid Sector, Broken Fingers, Glass Barbeque, Aurora Seven and Cockroach Diocese. “Ruin Value” is Empty Vessel’s first release to be reviewed on Side-Line.
items._genre: industrial / power electronics / cinematic / ritual ambient
items._cn_summary: 澳大利亚单人项目Empty Vessel首张专辑《Ruin Value》由Tom Wojcicki创作，2025年春通过德国地下厂牌Dunkelheit Produktionen发行限量CD与数字版。整张作品以八首曲目构建出极度压抑而密集的声场，将工业噪音、电影化配乐与仪式元素熔于一炉。打击乐处理如无人机般持续回响，制造出近乎窒息的听觉压迫感。曲目虽具重复性，但凭借强烈的密度与张力，将听者困入由扭曲影像与幻觉编织的声网之中。专辑作为整体呈现出连贯的高强度叙事，每一首都可视为独立的听觉事件。作为厂牌首批评论对象，此作展现出罕见的个人化声音语言，融合了身体性的工业冲击与氛围化的仪式美学，是该领域一次值得关注的声音探索。

items.body: Label: Sunnyside Records, 2026 Personnel - Jason Rigby: tenor and soprano saxophones; Lisa Parrott: alto, soprano, and baritone saxophones; Russ Johnson: trumpet; Cameron Brown: bass; Tony Jefferson: drums. Bassist and composer Cameron Brown has always felt comfortable in both traditional and avant-garde settings, and was an important element in the rhythm sections behind Archie Shepp, Don Pullen, George Adams, George Russell, Dewey Redman, and Don Cherry. Here, he leads a chordless quintet, paying tribute to Cherry as well as his mentor Dannie Richmond, best known for his extensive work with the one-and-only bassist, composer, and bandleader Charles Mingus. This ensemble started as a quartet featuring saxophonist Jason Rigby, trumpeter Russ Johnson, and drummer Tony Jefferson. Saxophonist Lisa Parrott joins them here for a dense, unfiltered session recorded live in concert in 2011. Raw and dense, it often sounds like a jam. The uptempo “ Sheila, It’s You! ”—written for the late jazz vocalist Sheila Jordan—has the three-horn frontline blowing with hard-bop intensity over the hard-charging swing provided by the rhythm section. They alternate solos before intersecting their searing lines with purpose. Conversely, “ Lullaby For George, Don, and Donnie ” is a 3/4 ballad gently propelled by brushes. “ Baby Suite ” is a through-composed response to Cherry’s “cocktail suite” concept. Brown’s three-minute bass monologue—featuring double-stops and thoughtful melodic development—right after the contrapuntal theme leads into faster bass circularity, with Jefferson free to embellish while the horns float above. A spontaneous avant-garde freedom reminiscent of Mingus’ excursions can be felt in the coda that precedes the theme. “ Cocktail Suite ”, which clocks in at 21 minutes and includes Cherry’s “ Remembrance ” and “ OC/DC ”, Jobim’s “ Portrait in Black and White ”, and Redman’s “ Mushi Mushi ”, features some awkward passages and elongated solos with the horns left to roam freely. Incessant walking lines populate the recording, creating an inescapable sense of anticipation. Brown’s “ Rylie’s Bounce ” blooms with a bass solo at the outset and explosive drumming by Jefferson, who throws in some barbed percussive sounds on Richmond’s “ Soft Seas ”, an amusing calypso dance served with humor and panache. Parrott causes some frisson on baritone, while Rigby explores the opposite end of the spectrum on soprano. This piece is put together much more effectively, with a keen sense of time and a divergence from conventional swing. With the interplay controlled at all times and the recording sounding like a classic, Remembrance sometimes rings a bit meandering, yet never disjointed. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Baby Suite ► 03 - Soft Seas ► 07 - Cocktail Suite
items._cn_summary: 贝斯手兼作曲家Cameron Brown领衔无和弦五重奏，向Don Cherry和导师Dannie Richmond致敬。2011年的现场录音呈现出原始而密集的质感，三支管乐在硬波普与自由爵士之间游走。《Sheila, It's You!》以快节奏硬摆动配合三条线索的热烈交叉对位；《Lullaby For George, Don, and Donnie》则是以刷子轻拂推进的三拍子叙事。《Baby Suite》采用通谱写法，Brown的贝斯独白以双音与旋律发展为前导，随后进入更快的循环段落，Jefferson自由装饰，铜管悬浮其上。《Cocktail Suite》长达21分钟，整合Cherry的多首作品及Jobim与Redman的作品，包含一些略显笨拙的段落与延伸独奏。Brown的《Rylie's Bounce》以贝斯开场配合Jefferson爆裂鼓声，Richmond的《Soft Seas》则是带有幽默气质的加力索舞曲，Parrott的低音萨克斯制造紧张感，Rigby的高音萨克斯探索对立音色。整体而言，控制得当的互动与近乎经典般的录音质感相互交织，偶尔略显散漫却从不失联。

items.body: Review by Chaoticreason — 4 .5 stars.It is difficult to add any more eloquent words than Fernando has already said. It took me more than a few plays to grasp this work. That is a good thing, all too often find something immediately likeable, then wonder why I liked it a week later I hate it. However, this album has longevity, as I also believe the band has.This is a band that will stay the course, with the brilliant, and classically trained Nat Bergrin at the helm, this music is a true delight for all fans of the more progressive/experimental side of rock.Whilst I think it's fair to say that most of us love retro-sounding bands, you will only get glimpses of that from this most excellent and progressive of albums.When I first played disc, I thought "Oh wow!" a garage rock band playing very complex prog rock, which I do still stand by in some ways. But the technicality of all the players involved pushes it well beyond a garage rock band in any conventional sense. I love that they are a not a paint by numbers neo rock band. This is a band pushing musical boundaries, and I love the direction that they are taking. I love their earlier album 'Heart of a Cherry Pit Sun', but this album enters a whole new realm. This is an album well worth checking out, if your penchant is for progressive Jazz, Classical, black metal... etc. etc....In fact, if you really love the progression of progressive rock music, then this is not a band to be missed.
items._genre: RIO / avant-prog / experimental rock / jazz-classical fusion
items._cn_summary: 这是一张需要多次聆听才能消化其全貌的前卫摇滚专辑，评论者特意指出其具备持久的耐听度，区别于初次即讨喜却经不起时间检验的速朽之作。乐队由古典训练背景的Nat Bergrin领军，音乐展现出极强的技术性和复杂程度，所有乐手的演奏将乐队推远超车库摇滚的范畴。专辑横跨前卫爵士、古典、黑金属等多个领域的审美边界，不满足于做按部就班的新派复古摇滚，而是持续拓展音乐的边界。评论者认为该作品相比乐队前作《Heart of a Cherry Pit Sun》进入了全新的维度，适合真正热爱前卫摇滚演进脉络的听众深入探索。整体制作理念倾向于跨界融合与持续实验，与学院派爵士及当代古典的审美取向高度契合。

items.body: One half of the Senior Staff was able to get out to a wholly non-ID:UD related gig over the weekend and catch Calgary’s Mares Of Thrace play a very rhythmically tight and cathartic set of doom metal. As we’ve briefly discussed here and there we’re both fans of a decent amount of metal covering a number of sub-genres, but neither of us are experts. Frankly, sometimes its nice to switch off the part of your brain that needs to be developing informed opinions and producing thoughtful analysis at all times and just enjoy some music simply because you dig it. But speaking of thoughtful analysis (?), let’s get you back to the home front with this week’s tracks. Dismantled Godflesh, “Master And Slave” Justin Broadrick announced earlier this year that he’d be winding Godflesh down for a second time some fifteen-odd years after its reactivation, but was planning two full LPs of new material before that time comes. The first such record sees release on Friday, and while the ratio of dub, electronic, and breaks elements which have always flitted about Godflesh releases had perhaps increased over the last few post-reunion albums, it’s hard not to think that Decay will be going right for the jugular Streetcleaner style based on its opening track. Turn it up and revel in the soothing annihilation of that bass tone. Decay by GODFLESH Grendel, “Dominion” It’s somehow been 7 years since the release of Grendel’s last LP Ascending the Abyss. It’s been a tangible absence in Our offices; JD Tucker has spent the last decade and a half redefining his legacy as an electro-industrial stylist and producer, starting with 2012’s genre-defying Timewave: Zero and the superlative Age of the Disposable Body, the latter being legitimately one of the most important political albums of the 2010s in Our Thing. “Dominion” speaks to the band we’ve come to know Grendel to be while showing some intriguing developments, such as JD’s now accomplished melodic vocal style, some very smooth string programming and sleek modern sound design applied to a classic EBM gallop. All that and lyrics that don’t just decry the social media era but examine the panopticon of control they emerge from? Welcome back Grendel, we missed you. Dominion by Grendel Dismantled, “Zero” Speaking of long-awaited returns, holy shit, there’s new Dismantled. Gary Zon’s long-running project has always been a standard bearer for a version of hard and harsh electro-industrial that maintains the genre’s atmospheric and emotional core. The first track from the forthcoming Endless is “Zero”, a cut that features Zon’s distinctive processed and multi-layered vocals, samples, and some fine string programming for good measure. It’s melancholic, but after a more than half a decade wait (the album was originally teased all the way back in 2021), it’s a sound that feels right. Endless by Dismantled Rosetta Stone, “Shadowban” Porl King’s moved Rosetta Stone through a number of preceding modes since reactivating the legendary second wave of goth rock project as a solo joint seven years back. A forthcoming release looks to keep that trend going (the Executing Nostalgia title feels rather on the nose in that regard) – one half of it will be made up of classic goth covers, continuing in the tradition of Unerotica and last year’s Nothing Is Sacred, while the other half is originals. This first taste of the latter feels like a callback to a very different moment in King’s history, though: the claustrophobic and hazy bass fog of this cut’s a dead ringer for the post witch house loops and grooves which made up the bulk of the voluminous In Death It Ends catalog in the 2010s. Shadowban by Rosetta Stone Control Fields, “Black Anomaly” Some solidly chewy bass sits at the centre of the B-side of the debut single from Tbilisi producer Control Fields, but that’s not the only thing which has us flashing back to 90s EBM and dark electro. The combo of icy programming and classic “hacking the Gibson” style sampling on this goes down as smooth as a Jolt cola being slammed during an all night Quake LAN party. Friction Code by Control Fields Emmon, “Relics (Kris Baha remix)” Kris Baha is one of the most reliable producers that emerged from the techno-body moment, with his canny grasp of gnarly sound design and how to assemble peak time bangers making him a go-to remixer for many artists. For evidece of why and the results why not check out Baha’s mix for Emmon’s “Relics”, taking the pensive and punchy original and giving it a slick peak-time makeover that references breakbeat driven 90’s techno, some psytrance, and some seriously warped synthwork. This’ll singe your nosehairs if you aren’t careful, play loud with caution. The post Tracks: September 21st, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 本周推荐聚焦三组回归的工业/电子音乐人。Godflesh 以新专辑《Decay》开篇曲回归重型的工业金属根基，Justin Broadrick 计划在乐队再次休团前完成两张全长新作，低音音色压迫感强烈。Grendel 时隔七年推出新专辑，单曲《Dominion》在经典 EBM 节奏骨架上融入了成熟的旋律人声、弦乐编程与现代声音设计，歌词审视社交媒体时代的全景控制结构。Dismantled 的新专辑《Endless》等待逾五载，首支单曲《Zero》延续了 Gary Zon 多层处理人声与采样的标志性手法，弦乐编排为冰冷质感增添忧郁层次。整体选曲倾向硬质电子与工业传统内的自我更新，关注节奏张力与政治性主题的结合。

items.body: Band: Kraanerg | Album: Aria for Labellum Tongues | Genre: Avant-prog | Year: 2026 From: Minneapolis, USA | Label: Independent For fans of: Frank Zappa, Papangu, Sigh, Cardiacs Bandcamp Kraanerg is the brainchild of composer and multi-instrumentalist Nat Bergrin, and Aria for Labellum Tongues is their third full-length release (and their second as a full band). This was my first exposure to Kraanerg, and I was very impressed by what I encountered. Western classical music plays a massive role on this record, both in terms of instrumentation and structure. Plenty of bands will shoehorn in some violin, but not many display the ability to integrate classical influences quite like this band does. “Amargosa Raga” kicks the album off with strange, discordant guitar lines. The vocal line is surprisingly melodic for the harsh, microtonal backing, and there’s some great supporting saxophone. Classical elements play a significant role here as well, with violin and piano taking the lead on various passages. What began as a fairly harsh piece gradually evolves into a lush composition, evoking many of the Mellotron-heavy greats of the classic prog era, but run through a more modern and uncompromisingly weird lens. The title track comes next, with an onslaught of buzzy guitars, swooping strings, and tinkling vibraphone. The classical influences on this track tread a fine line between sweet and creepy, with the violin frequently adding a remorseful edge.  “Blessings in Silk, Saffron, and Naran-Ji” nearly feels like a new wave song in its opening moments. There’s a bright hopefulness, but that soon gives way to a stripped-back classical passage. Piano, violin, and scratchy clean guitar float about. The intensity of the song gradually swells with the addition of drums and wordless vocals, lifting everything upward, but with an underlying sense of tension. When rock elements eventually take the lead again, violin remains the most prominent instrument. There’s an irrepressible sense of drama, and the somewhat rough vocals feel genuinely emotional. This piece is followed by the only song under four minutes on the album, “Anguloa Virginalis (Um Rosto de Mulher)”. It’s a light and airy breather following the intensity of the previous song. Piano, vibraphone, and delicate percussion evoke loungey jazz. Gothic organ and distorted guitar kicks off “Iron Sign of the Masdevallia”. Syncopated drums and piano give this track a disorienting feel, and the dense arrangement is smothering. As the song enters an instrumental section, sax and piano both get ample time in the spotlight, each one painting a dramatic picture. Next, the song takes a surprisingly sunny turn, with piano plinking out over a (mostly) major-key backing. The guitars borrow a lot from punk, but just about everything else is more clearly indebted to classical music, which makes for an interesting contrast. This artsy punk-fusion continues as this epic enters its final few minutes. The chords become more chaotic and irregular, and the vocals become more unhinged. The music is intense, yet oddly joyous, like Cardiacs’ best work. The opening gothic passage comes back for a closing reprise, which ties things up beautifully. The album ends on its longest song, the 20-minute “Visible to the Wrong Faces”. In comparison to the storming tempo of the previous song, this one is quite restrained in its opening. Classical music predominates for the first few minutes, led by piano and saxophone. It isn’t until about four minutes in that any rock elements enter, when buzzing guitars and stomping drums begin to play supporting roles. When vocals finally enter, the music is noisy with a sense of carefully-crafted chaos. Vibraphone and violin support jangly, post-punk guitars, and the vocal melody draws from avant-garde music. Throughout this whole album, the band has shown that they are masters of textural variation and contrast, and the second half of this song is a prime example. Post-metal, classical music, and classic prog influences are all evident, and everything gels into a satisfying conclusion. Aria for Labellum Tongues is a highly ambitious and very successful musical statement. The blending of rock and classical structures is pulled off wonderfully, and each of the songs on this album feels thoughtfully put-together. It’s a long and challenging record, but it’s well worth your time. Score: 95/100
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由Nat Bergrin领衔的Avant-Prog专辑，将西方古典音乐的作曲逻辑深度融入前卫摇滚框架。专辑以不和谐吉他线条和微分音和声开场，配合小提琴、钢琴、萨克斯与颤音琴等编制，展现出对古典器乐语汇的扎实掌握。作品在戏剧性与张力构建上极具匠心，从哥特管风琴到朋克吉他音色的剧烈转换，显示了跨风格的编曲能力。爵士与 Lounge 元素点缀其中，使整体层次更为丰富。文本虽未完结，但已清晰呈现了专辑在古典与前卫摇滚之间寻找平衡点的艺术方向，对偏爱实验性与复杂结构的听众具有相当吸引力。独立厂牌发行，无商业降权。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的第二张专辑延续了首张作品的多元文化融合路线。他们最显著的特色在于全部使用自制的非常规乐器——包括用废旧材料制成的 tassofons、tilofons、clarinuts、didjerimou 等。这些自制乐器在录音中展现出出乎意料的音准精度和丰富音质。乐队将自制乐器的音色与各文化音乐传统巧妙匹配：克莱兹默风格的欢快旋律配以拟人化的单簧管音色与拉丁打击乐；cumbia 风格中西班牙合唱与浓郁拉丁节奏交织；非洲节拍段落则围绕木鱼、铃铛和钹构建层次；中东风格曲目则带有六十年代间谍片主题曲式的恍惚感。各曲目的即兴段落展现出乐队扎实的演奏功底。整张专辑传递出一种理念：音乐的诞生源于人类对节奏与旋律的普遍热爱，乐器只是载体。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.album: Tony Njoku ~ A World of Bodies on Fire
items.excerpt: Tony Njoku‘s recent work has moved between open-ended instrumental composition and song. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE continues this movement in a more intimate setting. items.body: Tony Njoku‘s recent work has moved between open-ended instrumental composition and song. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE continues this movement in a more intimate setting. Across four pieces, piano, synthesisers and space provide the foundations of the music. The title track establishes the EP’s sound through layers of synthesiser harmonies that gather pace but stop short of a conventional climax. “Streams and Storms” turns towards private reflection, while “The Quiet Chaos of Playing It Safe” holds onto its tension without seeking a dramatic release. “Etude No. 1” strips the music down again, bringing the record to a sombre close. As Njoku explains in the accompanying interview, his move away from language is connected to an interest in how music can communicate feelings before they have been organised into words. Grief, exhaustion and recovery remain unresolved, expressed through harmony, resonance, dynamics and space. Small harmonic changes assume greater significance within these sparse arrangements. This is no suite in four movements, with constrasting character and same key signature. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE is a protean EP that searches and digs inwards, taking unexpected turns without any desire to dazzle. There is no show-off moment, no virtuoso display demanding attention, nor any grand moment of portending grief; emotion remains understated and kept in check. The music is unafraid of intimacy, allowing sustained harmonies, shifts in density and silence to determine its course, leaving much of the experience behind these compositions unspoken. To help us put out the fire we reached out directly to Tony Njoku for an interview conducted via email. All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was a large-scale collaborative statement concerned with spiritual preparedness, cultural resistance and collective survival, while the Bloom releases increasingly embraced instrumental composition, chamber arrangements and themes of grief, memory and renewal. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels like a further step in that direction: intensely personal, largely wordless and driven by the need to work through difficult emotions rather than narrative. Do you see this EP as the culmination of a journey that began with those recent releases, or did it emerge from a fundamentally different place? I don’t think of it as a culmination so much as another point of arrival. Each project tends to emerge from whatever questions I’m living with at the time. All Our Knives… was very outward-facing. It was about community, about bringing different voices into conversation around ideas of resilience and collective memory. Bloom and the instrumental work that followed became quieter spaces where I could sit with loss, change and the slower work of transformation. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE came from an even more internal place. I wasn’t trying to tell a story or resolve anything. I was more interested in documenting a state of being and exorcising some pent-up feelings that were essentially causing me harm. The music became a way of staying present with difficult emotions rather than translating them into language. In that sense it feels connected to the recent releases, but I wasn’t consciously trying to complete a trilogy or close a chapter. It simply became the form those experiences needed. One of the recurring threads across recent works—from The Loops (Grief) and Looking For Light to the standalone single “Malaise”—is an engagement with emotional turbulence that is neither entirely despairing nor entirely hopeful. The title track of A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE speaks of moving through fire rather than escaping it. Has your understanding of grief, burnout and recovery changed over the course of these releases, and do you think this EP arrives at a different emotional destination than those earlier works? I think grief has become less about something to overcome and more about something you learn to live alongside. Earlier work probably carried a stronger desire to find resolution or to move towards the light. I don’t think I see it that way anymore. Recovery isn’t linear, and neither is burnout. There are moments of joy inside exhaustion and moments of uncertainty inside healing. The image of moving through fire rather than escaping it felt important because some experiences can’t be bypassed. They change you. The music on this EP isn’t trying to extinguish the fire; it’s trying to understand what remains after you’ve passed through it. If there’s hope here, it’s a quieter kind. It’s found in endurance, attention and the possibility of continuing to create despite everything. One of the striking aspects of All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was the way you brought together an extraordinary community of Black British voices—Tricky, GAIKA, Ghostpoet, Coby Sey, James Massiah, Space Afrika, Labi Junior and others—creating a record that felt simultaneously personal and collective. More broadly, your recent work has moved freely between songs, spoken-word collaborations, chamber-like compositions, ambient electronics and abstract instrumental forms. By contrast, A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels almost entirely self-contained, built around piano, synthesisers and extended instrumental pieces. After such a collaborative album, did the absence of other voices create a different kind of honesty or vulnerability? Collaboration has always been fundamental to my practice because it allows ideas to exist beyond my own perspective. All Our Knives… couldn’t have existed without those voices. The conversations between people were the point of the record. With this EP I found myself needing the opposite experience. I needed solitude, not because I wanted to withdraw from community, but because I needed to hear what was underneath all the noise. Working mostly alone meant there was nowhere to hide. Every hesitation, every silence, every decision belonged to me. That can feel vulnerable, but it can also be very freeing because you’re no longer trying to explain yourself through words or through other people’s interpretations. I also needed space to cry and I find that’s a hard thing for me to do in front of people, I let go of my masks the most in solitude. So it became a conversation with the instruments themselves. The piano, synthesizers and space all became collaborators in a different sense. You’ve described this EP as a collection of “raging exhalations, quiet revelations, subtle smirks of humility, laments and meditations.” Unlike many of your previous releases, there are no guest vocalists, no lyrics and no obvious narrative anchors. Did working without words feel liberating or exposing? And at this stage in your career, do you feel instrumental music has become just as capable as song of carrying the political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always been central to your work? Working without words was both liberating and exposing. Lyrics can sometimes direct people towards a particular meaning, whereas instrumental music leaves much more room for the listener’s own experience. That openness was something I wanted to embrace. I’ve become increasingly interested in what music communicates before language enters. Breath, texture, resonance, silence… these things carry meaning too. They can hold emotion in ways that words sometimes can’t. I don’t really separate instrumental music from song anymore. They’re just different ways of asking the same questions. The political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always interested me don’t disappear when language disappears. They become embodied differently. Sometimes a sustained note or a shift in harmony can express something that would become smaller if I tried to explain it. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by AshleyLarksTongue — This album is quite an acquired taste. I hated it at first, and hated it even more every listen after. It took me 20 listens before I started even tolerating it. However, after 30 listens, I can say it's a masterpiece of avant-prog. The Captain's voice has really grown on me, and so has the wonderful musicianship. My favorite track and the most essential track off of this album is sweet sweet bulbs. I really have no idea how to say more about this album because it is simply indescribable. I'm looking forward to exploring some more of Beefheart's works. And everyone around me now has to deal with me doing my impression of the hilarious vocals on this album.
items._cn_summary: 这张1969年的前卫专辑以极其怪诞的手法挑战听众的听觉习惯。评论者经历了从厌恶到容忍再到认可的过程，最终在反复聆听约三十次后将其视为前卫摇滚中的杰作。专辑的器乐演奏极为出色，Captain Beefheart的嗓音独特且充满表现力，尽管最初令人难以接受，但最终展现出强大的吸引力。专辑中最具代表性的曲目是《Sweet Sweet Bulbs》，被视为理解整张作品的关键。整体而言，这是一张难以用语言精确描述的实验性作品，其价值需要通过反复聆听才能逐渐显现，对前卫音乐爱好者而言具有重要的探索意义。

items.body: German medieval techno act Klangschmiede & Friends released the single “Remember” on September 1, 2026, and submitted it as an application for Germany’s national selection process for the Eurovision Song Contest 2027. The full application was uploaded to public broadcaster SWR on the same day; German participation in the 2027 contest is not yet confirmed. Live bagpipes, hurdy-gurdy and flute sit alongside electronic production on “Remember,” with English lyrics and passages in Old High German drawn from early medieval sources such as the Hildebrandslied. The track runs just under three minutes and moves between medieval techno, dark electronic production and historical folk balladry. Klangschmiede & Friends’ Eurovision 2027 bid For the submission, Klangschmiede expanded into the extended line-up Klangschmiede & Friends, bringing in additional musicians for the song’s acoustic instrumentation. The official music video was filmed with the full ensemble at Schloss Burg in Solingen on August 17, 2026. Regional public broadcaster WDR was on site for the shoot and aired a television feature on the production through its Lokalzeit Bergisches Land program. The submission has also drawn coverage from ESC kompakt and regional newspapers including the Solinger Tageblatt and the Remscheider General-Anzeiger. About Klangschmiede Klangschmiede is the duo of Claudia Sokoll and Timo Tofaute, based in the Bergisches Land region of Germany and operating officially since 2025. The project mixes medieval and Nordic folk elements with electronic production, drawing on historical sources such as the Hildebrandslied, the Poetic Edda and Nordic ballads. Its catalog includes the album “RITUS”, released digitally and on CD on May 14, 2026, and singles including “Nothing We Love Is Ever Gone” (March 26, 2026), “Hüter der Straße” (April 30, 2026) and “Solringen” (July 23, 2026), alongside a remix of “Tanz den Feuertanz” featuring Keltania. Klangschmiede has also worked with the medieval folk-rock band Corvus Corax on the track “Ragnarök”. “Remember”, released as a single on September 1, 2026 under the expanded name Klangschmiede & Friends, is the project’s submission for Germany’s national Eurovision Song Contest 2027 selection, with participation still to be confirmed.

items.album: The Sound Veil Society: ‘We will always aim to be as honest and raw in our expression’
items.excerpt: The Sound Veil Society‘s debut album “Things We Kept” is built around an unusual kind of intensity. items.body: The Sound Veil Society‘s debut album “Things We Kept” is built around an unusual kind of intensity. The record rarely reaches for aggression or dramatic excess; instead, emotional weight accumulates through restraint, space, repetition and the careful relationship between voice, electronics and silence. That became even clearer to me after seeing the duo at E-Only before spending more time with the album. Live, the songs seemed capable of becoming physically larger without sacrificing the intimacy they carry on record. The Swedish-Norwegian project brings together Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson, two musicians with extensive histories in Nordic electronic music, but “Things We Kept” does not sound like an exercise in accumulated experience or genre expertise. The more interesting question is what happens when experience becomes instinct: when musicians know enough to stop demonstrating what they know and instead concentrate on what a song actually needs. Released on 11 September 2026 through Progress Productions, “Things We Kept” is the duo’s first full-length album. Its title becomes more revealing as the record unfolds. What we keep is not necessarily what we consciously choose to preserve. Memory, grief, unfinished conversations, attachments and previous versions of ourselves remain present long after circumstances have changed. That tension between movement and emotional permanence runs quietly through an album whose apparent delicacy repeatedly turns out to carry considerable force. The Sound Veil Society interview Karo: I saw you at E-Only before hearing “Things We Kept”, and what struck me was that the performance generated enormous emotional pressure without relying on aggression or theatrical excess. Is restraint something you consciously build into The Sound Veil Society, or is it simply where the two of you naturally meet? The Sound Veil Society: It’s the natural way for us to express ourselves, and TSVS is the outlet where we can give these feelings and emotions free space in our performance, both on record and live. Karo: “Things We Kept” is a debut album made by musicians who are anything but beginners. Does starting a new project after years of experience give you greater freedom, or does experience make it harder to surprise yourselves because you already know too well what works? The Sound Veil Society: Good question! In a way, it gives us more freedom, as we use our experience together with what we have learned over the years to create something new. But it might just be the circle of life, as we evolve through different phases in our lives, with new experiences and so on. And it would be boring to repeat ourselves, so to trigger creativity and motivation, we just do what we like and hopefully someone else likes it as well. Karo: The album feels remarkably coherent across music, lyrics, photography, videos and the physical booklet. Did you think of “Things We Kept” as a complete world from the beginning, or did that visual and emotional language gradually reveal itself while the music was taking shape? The Sound Veil Society: We did have an idea from the beginning to be very visual in what we do as TSVS. The album itself is a result of our journey in making it. After a year or so of making a lot of demos, we decided where we wanted to take our sound, and after that everything just fell into place. “Things We Kept” became a complete world through the process and, indeed, there is a thought behind the booklet, videos and music completing each other. Karo: There is something almost paradoxical about this record: it sounds delicate, but never weak. I kept thinking of tempered glass: transparent, apparently fragile, yet internally capable of carrying enormous force. Where does that balance between vulnerability and strength come from in your writing? The Sound Veil Society: Really like your reflection of the record! It reflects quite well who we are as people, in a way, as both of us are emotional beings, with our share of struggles both in the past and present. But that can also be used as a strength, because you need a certain amount of strength to deal with the challenges in life. So for us it is a very natural process and nothing we “try” to do. It just happens that way. Karo: The lyrics repeatedly return to movement: leaving, running, waiting, returning, searching for air. Yet emotionally, many of the characters seem unable to escape what they carry with them. Were you consciously interested in the difference between physically moving on and actually changing? The Sound Veil Society: Not really. It is just our way of describing thoughts and feelings that are close to us, or stories and reflections that have inspired us over the years. Karo: The title “Things We Kept” becomes more interesting the longer one spends with the record, because what people keep is often not something they would consciously choose: grief, unfinished conversations, versions of other people, even destructive attachments. What does “keeping” mean to you in the context of this album? The Sound Veil Society: We think that everything we experience, be it good or bad, stays with us to some degree, even when we have almost forgotten about it, because it shapes us into who we are right now. Without all the experiences we go through in life, we would not be the same people we are today. Karo: Erlend’s voice is very exposed in these songs, but the arrangements rarely try to underline every emotion he expresses. How do you decide when the music should support the voice and when it should deliberately leave it almost alone? The Sound Veil Society: It’s all about the feeling, really, and nothing we think too much about when we make music. To express ourselves the way we want, it just tends to become like that. Karo: One thing I noticed both at E-Only and on the album is how important space is. The songs are not afraid of air, pauses or sounds that are allowed to remain isolated. In electronic music, where it is technically very easy to keep adding layers, is knowing what to remove as important to you as knowing what to write? The Sound Veil Society: In a way it is, but the most important thing for us is to write a good song and express the feeling we want to express with it. We do use quite a lot of layers, but they are often subtle and just there to emphasise the sound. Since we have some years behind us making music, we have learned that sometimes less is more. Karo: The visual material often uses roads, water, landscapes, silhouettes and people partly disappearing from view. They feel less like illustrations of individual songs than fragments of memory. How closely do you work on the relationship between image and sound, and what can an image express that you deliberately leave unresolved in the lyrics? The Sound Veil Society: It depends on the idea of the song we are working on, but we often get visual ideas while making music. An image or a video clip itself is a great way to describe emotions, and combining sound and visuals simply makes a story more complete. Karo: Your musical backgrounds give you access to an established electronic vocabulary, yet “Things We Kept” does not sound interested in demonstrating genre knowledge. Was there anything from your previous projects that you consciously had to unlearn in order for The Sound Veil Society to develop its own identity? The Sound Veil Society: Not much, really. The only thing we have been trying to do is shorten parts, as it is easy to keep things simply because they sound good, but in the end they often just make a track less interesting. Other than that, everything else just fell into place during the making of it. Karo: At E-Only I had the impression that some of these songs actually became larger through performance without losing their intimacy. Has playing the material in front of people changed your understanding of the album, perhaps shown you emotional qualities in certain songs that were less obvious in the studio? The Sound Veil Society: It can happen, but we often already have an idea of how a song will work live when we make it. So most of our work is made just as much for the live stage as it is for a record, actually. Of course, before the first live show, we didn’t know how our vision would translate to the audience, but after these shows we really feel that we get a special connection with the audience. Karo: “Things We Kept” establishes a very precise emotional and visual identity for a first album. Looking ahead, does that identity now feel like a foundation you want to deepen, or something you already feel tempted to disturb? What are you curious to discover about The Sound Veil Society next? The Sound Veil Society: In a way, it is a foundation to build upon and is, in many ways, the core of our concept. But we do want to evolve and make something new along the way, so we don’t yet know what it will become. But that is also part of the fun: exploring new sides of a concept. We will always aim to be as honest and raw in our expression. About The Sound Veil Society The Sound Veil Society is a Swedish-Norwegian electronic duo formed in 2024 by Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson. Eilertsen is associated with Essence Of Mind and Lights A.M. and joined Xenturion Prime in 2024; Mattsson co-founded Code 64, later established Xenturion Prime and has also been involved with Essence Of Mind. The project debuted with “The River” on 24 April 2025, followed by “OK” on 22 August 2025 and “Hunger for Light” in March 2026. Their debut album, “Things We Kept”, was released by Progress Productions on 11 September 2026. The standard edition contains eleven tracks, including “Voices” featuring KÅRP; the CD adds three bonus versions, while the album was also issued on black-and-white splatter vinyl and as a limited MiniDisc edition. The duo performed at Nocturnal Culture Night and E-Only Festival; a live video for “Nothing to Say” was recorded at E-Only in Leipzig in March 2026. The Sound Veil Society are already confirmed for Eastside Festival in Halle (Saale), Germany, on 2-3 July 2027.
items._cn_summary: The Sound Veil Society由瑞典和挪威音乐人组成，首张专辑《Things We Kept》以克制、空间与重复为美学核心。评论指出，专辑通过人声、电子声响与沉默之间的精细关系积累情感重量，而非依赖侵略性或戏剧化手法。在E-Only现场的观看进一步印证了这种特质——现场表演能将情感张力放大，却不牺牲录音中固有的亲密感。专辑标题"Things We Kept"暗指那些无意识留存的事物——记忆、悲伤、未竟的对话与过去的自我版本，这一主题贯穿始终。乐评以采访形式展开，成员谈到经验与自由的关系：多年积累的北欧电子音乐背景并未让作品沦为对经验的展示，而是让技艺转化为直觉，专注于歌曲本身的需要。整体呈现安静却暗含强大力量的聆听体验。

items.body: Purest Form Resistance Dais Records Despite its brief fifteen minute runtime, there’s a meal to be made out of LA trio Purest Form’s latest EP, their debut on Dais, both in terms of attitude and presentation, as well as what its selection of very clear influences might portend for the larger post-industrial landscape. Drawing upon familiar markers of 90s electronic aggression, Resistance provides a tight test case for their read on that historical moment. Opener “Animal” functions as a strong calling card for Purest Form, showing both their capacity for a catchy, heavily processed guitar riff as well as Story Beeson’s acidic growl that’s part grindcore, part death metal. Factor in just the right amount of backing programming and an easily chantable chorus and it becomes both cathartic and anthemic in short order. It is, to be glib, exactly the type of thrashing industrial rock glory which KMFDM have been failing to recapture for the past couple of decades. Much of the rest of the EP’s made up of densely programmed two-minute wipeouts jammed up with breaks, more heavily processed guitar now functioning more for colour than riffs, and more spleen and vile being vented. If that sounds on paper fairly akin to digital hardcore, listening to “Break” and “More” will do little to dissuade that presumption. “Beyond Terror” acts as a quick riposte to this frenetic pace, offering post-hardcore chug while the vocals cut through equivocations about the killings of Palestinians – “call it what you like, it’s genocide.” And then there’s the closing cover. Fifteen or twenty years back, an industrial metal act doing a straightforward version of The Prodigy’s “Breathe” would have felt awkwardly retrograde. However, a full three decades on from the original release and overdriven into the red to the point that it’s difficult to distinguish original tracks from sampled ones, Purest Form’s take on “Breathe” feels like the best sort of “oh shit, they’re covering this?” moment at the end of a packed and sweaty basement show. In discussing the appeal of the 90s sources Pures Form borrow from it’s important to not overstate how new they might be to the band; both Beeson and guitarist/programmer Madi Woodward both have lengthy rap sheets with slews of hardcore and metal acts going back a decade or so. But there’s no question that a combination of their backgrounds beyond industrial and the historical space separating Resistance from those acts helps invigorate their dense and furious angle on them. Buy it. RESISTANCE by PUREST FORM The post Purest Form, “Resistance” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: Purest Form 这张短篇 EP 仅有十五分钟，却以密集编排的工业电子攻击性见长。开篇曲展示经过重度处理的吉他 riff 与 grindcore / death metal 风格的嘶吼嗓音，加上精准的编程节拍与易记副歌，在短暂篇幅内实现了宣泄感与 anthem 式的张力。后续曲目多为两分钟左右的密集编程冲撞，融合数字硬核的急促节奏与破碎切分。第七首插入巴勒斯坦议题的政治文本，以 post-hardcore 律动承载直接呐喊。结尾翻唱 The Prodigy 的经典曲目，将原作过载至红区边界，使采样与原创元素难以分辨。乐评指出乐队成员此前活跃于硬核与金属圈，因此对这些九十年代素材的演绎并非简单复古，而是带有外部视角的新鲜融合。整体定位接近九十年代工业金属的复兴路线，独立厂牌发行，态度鲜明。

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了1978至1983年间自动音乐作曲家联盟（League of Automatic Music Composers）的作品，是早期计算机音乐与即兴演奏交汇的珍贵文献。评论者原本预期这些45年前的电脑音乐会显得晦涩过时，但实际聆听后发现其具有独特的吸引力。作品以算法生成与人类即兴互动为核心机制，演奏者在计算机程序产生的结构框架中进行实时回应与操控，探索了机器与人之间的创作边界。作为先锋派电脑音乐的重要历史档案，本合辑不仅具有学术价值，也展现了早期算法作曲在声音探索上的前瞻性。整体呈现出密集而耐人寻味的聆听体验，适合对音乐技术史与声音实验感兴趣的听众深入探索。

items.body: Valencia label Industrial Complexx reissues the various-artists compilation “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends” on double cassette and digital on October 15, 2026. The 18-track set, originally released by Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, gathers international minimal synth, electro-punk and industrial acts covering the catalogue of Suicide’s Alan Vega and Martin Rev. SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends by Various Artists The reissue accompanies the Spanish-language publication of “Suicide, delincuentes electrónicos,” an essay on the band by musician and writer Pedro Peñas y Robles, originally published in French and English in 2024 and now released in Spanish by Industrial Complexx. The book traces the duo’s genesis and the chaotic sessions behind their 1977 debut album, drawing on testimony from scene figures including Marc Hurtado of Étant Donnés. ‘SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends’ contributors The tribute pairs Vega and Rev’s original catalogue with reinterpretations from Distel, Radical G, The Horrorist, David Carretta and Jürgen Engler of Die Krupps, Növö, Adan+Ilse featuring Gabi Delgado of D.A.F., Marc Hurtado performing with Alan Vega himself, Liebknecht featuring Kristoffer Grip of Agent Side Grinder, Unknown Celebrities, Laag, Position Parallele, Cruise [ctrl] featuring Richard 23 and Patrick Codenys of Front 242, The Present Moment, Absolute Body Control, Millimetric featuring Dirk Da Davo of The Neon Judgement, Black Egg featuring hausfrau, Simi Nah featuring KGB, and In Death It Ends featuring Usher of Norma Loy. Covered songs include “Che,” “Ghost Rider,” “Cheree,” “Frankie Teardrop,” “Dream Baby Dream” and “Diamonds, Fur Coat, Champagne.” Industrial Complexx describes the collection as channeling “the same abrasive, alienating and futuristic energy” that shaped Suicide’s catalogue. About Suicide Suicide was an American duo formed in New York City in 1970 by vocalist Alan Vega and instrumentalist Martin Rev, initially a trio with guitarist Paul Liebgott before continuing as a two-piece. The group paired Vega’s stream-of-conscious, rockabilly-inflected vocals with Rev’s minimal synthesizer and drum-machine backing, and was among the first acts to use the term “punk music” to describe itself, in 1970. Suicide independently released its debut album, “Suicide,” in 1977 on Red Star Records, featuring “Ghost Rider,” “Frankie Teardrop” and “Cheree.” A second album, “Suicide: Alan Vega and Martin Rev,” followed in 1980 on Ze Records, then “A Way of Life” in 1988, “Why Be Blue” in 1992 and the final studio album, “American Supreme,” in 2002. Vega and Rev also worked separately: Vega collaborated with Andrew Eldritch of The Sisters of Mercy as The Sisterhood in 1986, and with Alex Chilton and Ben Vaughn on “Cubist Blues” in 1996, while both released solo albums throughout their careers. Suicide played its final concert at London’s Barbican Centre on July 9, 2015, before Alan Vega died on July 16, 2016, at age 78. “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends,” first released via Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, returns via Industrial Complexx on October 15, 2026, alongside the Spanish edition of Pedro Peñas y Robles’s book on the band.

items._cn_summary: 瓦伦西亚厂牌Industrial Complexx重新发行向纽约传奇二人组Suicide致敬的多艺术家合辑，以双卡带与数字形式推出。这套18首作品的合辑原由Unknown Pleasures Records于2014年发行，汇集了来自国际的极简合成器、电子朋克与工业厂牌，重新演绎Alan Vega与Martin Rev的曲目。参与翻唱的阵容包括Distel、The Horrorist、Jürgen Engler（Die Krupps）、Adan+Ilse联合Gabi Delgado（D.A.F.）、Marc Hurtado与Alan Vega本人、Dirk Da Davo（The Neon Judgement）等，涵盖"Che"、"Ghost Rider"、"Frankie Teardrop"等经典作品。再版同时伴随西班牙语版随笔《Suicide, delincuentes electrónicos》的发行。厂牌将这套合辑描述为传递Suicide作品中那种"磨蚀、疏离与未来感"的能量。作为一篇资讯类文章，缺乏对音乐本身的深度评析，但内容详实，聚焦于小众暗潮与工业领域的跨界致敬企划。

items.album: Charlie May / Trusted Farms (ASIPV058)
items.body:
After decades contributing to records where a single riff could transform a dancefloor, Charlie May turns that instinct inward on Trusted Farms. 

 For over thirty years, Charlie has occupied a position that seems increasingly rare in electronic music: the musician’s musician, the person behind the machines, the extra pair of hands in the studio, and quite often, the person responsible for the melody you end up carrying around in your head for weeks on end. 

 Alongside Duncan Forbes as Spooky, Charlie helped shape some of the most important electronic music to emerge from the UK in the early ’90s. That partnership would also sow the seeds for one of Sasha’s defining records: the central riff behind Xpander began life in Spooky’s live material, before Charlie brought the idea into the studio with Sasha and helped transform it into one of electronic music’s most enduring anthems.

 astrangelyisolatedplace · ASIPV058 Charlie May / Trusted Farms [PREVIEWS] 

 Listen closely to Charlie’s work and there’s a particular instinct that keeps returning: knowing when a simple synth line is enough. Knowing which note needs to change. Knowing when repetition stops being repetition and starts becoming the entire reason a track works. More recently, as one-third of Quiet Places on ASIP, he’s taken those same instincts somewhere looser — beatless, gridless and led by improvisation.

 Trusted Farms puts those instincts front and centre.

 Tiny melodic phrases appear and refuse to leave. Synth lines repeat just long enough to become lodged in your head. Parts rub against each other without being tidied into submission. There’s a sharpness and directness to it all amongst the purposeful analogue warmth.

 Some of these tracks feel almost ridiculously simple at first. But simplicity is difficult when you’ve spent decades learning every possible way to complicate something. Many of the parts on Trusted Farms were performed live with minimal editing. A synth line might be doubled, distorted, re-recorded and pushed back through another piece of equipment, but it remains the same idea. Instead of filling the gaps, Charlie works on the weight and character of what is already there. The melodies become physical; slightly worn around the edges.

 For someone whose fingerprints can be found across some genuinely monumental moments in electronic music, Charlie has spent decades knowing what to add. Trusted Farms is about knowing exactly what to leave alone.

 Available on black 12” and digital, mastered by Andreas Lupo LOOP-O Lubich and featuring artwork by Peter Skwiot Smith, Trusted Farms will be available on October 16th 2026.

items._cn_summary: Charlie May 在三十余年幕后生涯后推出首张个人专辑《Trusted Farms》，将舞曲制作中对单一钩子的敏锐直觉转向内省。专辑以极简合成器旋律为核心，短小的乐句反复循环后逐渐占据听者意识，不依赖结构堆叠，而是通过模拟设备的多次回录与叠加赋予旋律重量与磨损感。大量段落采用现场即兴录制，保留未驯服的摩擦与边缘。作为 Quiet Places 三人组成员，他近年已在 ASIP 厂牌探索无节拍网格的即兴领域，这张专辑则将那种松散感推至更聚焦的位置：知道何时该添加，更知道何时该放手。模拟温暖与锐利感并存，黑胶12寸由小众厂牌 A Strangely Isolated Place 发行。

items.body: Everybody Else’s Life, Too is the latest from Josh Berman, a stalwart of the Chicago scene still somewhat underappreciated outside of his hometown. He has played the gamut of Chicago improvisors (including Mars Williams’ A Very Ayler Xmas project, the all-too-short-lived Michael Zerrang and the Blue Lights, and Ken Vandermark’s Audio One), sneaked across the Atlantic to record with Paul Lytton, Edward Perraud, and Jon Rune Strøm, and led several of his own bands. On this one, he is joined by bassist Jason Roebke – a reliably punchy oft-times sideman of Chicago circles - and the indefatigable drummer Chris Corsano for a live date at Chicago’s Constellation from 2025. I cannot say there is much surprising here if you are familiar with Berman’s previous headline albums. That said, this is more of what this listener wants rather than simply more of the same. Berman clearly has a thing for bop, in its various forms, and maybe the title is even a nod to his appreciation of those who came before and inspired him. The songs on here start with a catchy head, or a few more plodding, smokey ones, and from there break down into spurs, knotty angles, and spindly striations. One could play this album for someone who thought Miles went too far when he went electric, or Coltrane with Ascension, and they would happily bob their head along with Roebke’s walking bass or Corsano’s steady patter behind Berman’s jumpy melodies. But restricting this to such a palatable bridge would miss the other point, which lies in the free form sections that, yes, are tied to the head but in a sensual way that deviates from its rhythm, tune, and key in favor of capturing, extending, and straining the intricacies of a spontaneous moment. Those sections are when Berman stretches into flutters, crackles, and bites, when Roebke leans into timbre, and Corsano eschews rhythm for sound. Those sections are limited; in this case I think for the better. That is not because trio cannot stretch out into the unknown. (Take the eighth cut, Scale, as an example of their exploratory chops.) Instead, it is because they do so within Berman’s bookending melodic confines that set the direction and mark the terminal point. And were those themes not inspired, this would fall flat. But they are and do not. For doubters, just listen to the wonderfully lonesome and wistful closer, Second Look, where Corsano’s brushes lay a soft-rain backdrop to Berman’s and Roebke’s melancholic dialog. Everybody Else’s Life, Too is much in the vein of a different Josh Berman Trio’s A Dance and a Hop (2015) and should be considered an expansion of that project. Again, you might well know what to expect if you have been following Berman already, but that does not make what you hear any less satisfying. Everybody Else’s Life, Too is available download from Bandcamp and a CD from a few choice independent music outlets. See the CvD website for more . items._cn_summary: Josh Berman 是芝加哥场景的中坚力量，此张专辑由低音提琴手 Jason Roebke 与鼓手 Chris Corsano 共同录制于2025年Constellation的现场。曲目以抓耳的bop式主题或缓慢烟雾感旋律开场，随后在自由即兴段落中解构节奏、调性与曲式。Berman 的吹奏呈现出颤音、碎裂声与短促咬音的纹理，Roebke 转向音色探索，Corsano 则脱离节拍框架转向声响本身。编曲策略将自由段落控制在主题框架之内，既留有即兴张力又不失方向感。第八首 Scale 是三人探索能力的集中展现，收尾曲 Second Look 以 Corsano 刷子的细雨底色衬托 Berman 与 Roebke 的忧郁对话。作为2015年专辑 A Dance and a Hop 的延续与扩展，整体风格成熟一致，对熟悉 Berman 的听众而言并不意外，但仍具满足感。

French soprano saxophonist and composer Emile Parisien is an eclectic jazz practitioner with inestimable musical gifts that allow him to explore a whole universe of sound. items.body: Label: ACT, 2026 Personnel - Emile Parisien: soprano saxophone; Yaron Herman: piano; Linda May Han Oh: bass; Prabhu Edouard: tabla, percussion, voice. French soprano saxophonist and composer Emile Parisien is an eclectic jazz practitioner with inestimable musical gifts that allow him to explore a whole universe of sound. Parisien brings a glowing selection of tunes composed by himself, pianist and longtime collaborator Yaron Herman, and proficient bassist Linda May Han Oh, alongside two covers. Rounding out the quartet is tabla player and vocalist Prabhu Edouard, who helps establish an organically integrated framework for the leader’s world-fusion aesthetics. This group was formed after a memorable first performance in Paris. Floating opens with Georges Ivanovitch Gurdjieff and Thomas de Hartmann’s “ Asian Songs & Rhythms, No. 40 ”, a peaceful, spiritual tune that, combining Eastern modal traditions with Western classical sensibilities, slowly unfolds with a ternary feel. Parisien employs his intervallic expertise in vibrant phrasing, while Herman evokes distant, serene landscapes. The other cover on the album is Anouar Brahem’s “ Badhra ”—the fantastic opening track of his trio album Thimar—which scintillates with sophistication and enchantment. In the latter, Herman’s clarity of speech and objectivity pair well with the in-and-out lyricism of Parisien, while the duo’s co-written piece, “ Portal ”, keeps the rhythmic momentum going after a dynamic introduction centered on Edouard, who doubles on tabla and voice. Herman’ piano solo on this one is pure delight. On the other hand, Parisien’s “ Bonbon ” is filled with excitement and aligned with Middle Eastern traditions. Herman contributes five compositions of his own: the waltzing ballads “ Olive Branch ” and “ Ruth ”, with the latter acquiring a jazzier, Keith Jarrett-esque vibe before morphing into a more percussive passage over which Parisien’s soprano glides effortlessly; the playful and bluesy “ Nusrat ”; and the stop-and-go flow of “ El Toro ”, a showcase for Oh’s rhythmic adroitness. Sandwiched between the latter two tracks is the bassist’s “ As It Comes And As It Goes ”, a moment of reflection and an opportunity to hear her unaccompanied. According to the bandleader, this is music about peace, poetry, and love, and listeners should be able to feel its emotional appeal as well as the group’s ability to communicate through whatever musical language they choose to mix in. This forward-looking diversity is key, and Parisien’s fusion is not without an airily contemporary touch. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Asian Songs & Rhythms, No 40 ► 04 - Badhra ► 08 - Nusrat
